entity: Arab members of OAPEC; OPEC; Egypt; Syria; Israel; United States; global oil-importing economies
summary: The first major oil shock followed the Yom Kippur War of 6–26 October 1973. After the United States resupplied Israel, Arab members of OAPEC announced an embargo against the United States and selected other countries, alongside production cuts. The price of oil rose from about US$2.90 per barrel before the embargo to US$11.65 by January 1974. The embargo was lifted in March 1974, but higher prices and the economic shock persisted.
why: The war was the immediate geopolitical trigger, but the crisis also reflected pre-existing tensions over oil pricing, producer power, supply capacity and the growing dependence of industrial economies on imported petroleum. The embargo and production cuts transmitted a supply shock through energy, transport, manufacturing, inflation, trade balances and financial markets.
impact: The United States, Japan and Western European oil importers faced shortages, higher energy costs, inflation and recessionary pressure. India also experienced a severe oil-price shock; the RBI's historical chronology records quadrupled oil prices, double-digit inflation and a global recession. Oil-exporting states received a major transfer of income. The map distinguishes the war's political centres, oil-producing decision centres and selected financial/industrial centres exposed to the shock; it does not imply that each location was equally affected.

title: Thailand floats the baht
entity: Bank of Thailand; Government of Thailand
summary: On 2 July 1997, Thailand abandoned its exchange-rate peg and allowed the baht to float after mounting pressure on its currency and foreign-exchange reserves. The move became the opening trigger in the Asian financial crisis, which spread through several economies in the region.
why: The episode exposed vulnerabilities linked to short-term foreign borrowing, currency mismatches, weak financial-sector balance sheets and pressure on fixed exchange-rate regimes. Thailand entered an IMF-supported adjustment programme in August 1997. The crisis then affected Indonesia, Korea and other regional markets, although each country experienced its own sequence of events.
impact: The downturn brought recession, financial-sector restructuring and significant social strain across affected economies. The IMF's retrospective account reports that Thailand's real GDP fell by more than 10% in 1998. This record describes the regional crisis trigger; it does not imply that every later consequence occurred in Bangkok itself.

title: The Dot-Com Bubble Burst (2000–2002)
entity: NASDAQ; technology companies; venture capital markets
summary: Technology shares peaked on 10 March 2000 before a prolonged collapse in internet and technology valuations. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 77% from its peak by October 2002, as speculative business models, high valuations and financing conditions unwound.
why: The episode exposed the risks of valuing growth companies on expectations without durable earnings or cash flows. The repricing affected venture funding, IPO markets, technology employment and equity portfolios.
impact: The technology-company concentration around Silicon Valley and the trading and capital-raising ecosystem in New York were two important nodes; the repricing spread internationally.

why: Lehman's collapse was not the sole cause of the global financial crisis. Its failure disrupted counterparties and confidence across interconnected financial markets.
impact: The crisis contributed to a deep global recession, rising unemployment, business failures, foreclosures and household financial distress. region: Persian Gulf; Middle East; global energy markets
entity: Iran; Israel; United States; Gulf oil and gas exporters; International Energy Agency; global oil-importing economies

summary: On 28 February 2026, the United States and Israel began military strikes against Iran. Iran retaliated across the region, and the Strait of Hormuz—through which roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of seaborne oil and petroleum-product trade normally passes—was effectively closed to much commercial traffic. The disruption cut Gulf exports, raised shipping and insurance costs, and sent crude prices sharply higher. The International Energy Agency coordinated a record emergency stock release, while producers and traders sought alternative routes and supplies. By September, renewed hostilities and depleted inventories again put upward pressure on prices. As of 9 November 2026, oil flows had partly recovered and prices had fallen sharply in the prior week, but attacks on shipping and the absence of a comprehensive settlement meant geopolitical risk remained.
why: This shock combined a military conflict with a chokepoint disruption. The Strait of Hormuz is a critical route for Gulf crude, refined products and LNG. Reduced traffic affected exporters and importers, while rerouting, stock releases, alternative production and weaker demand softened—but did not eliminate—the supply shock. The effects spread through fuel prices, freight, aviation, petrochemicals, inflation expectations, trade balances and financial markets.
impact: The Gulf states faced disrupted exports and energy infrastructure risks. Oil-importing economies in Asia—including India, Japan, South Korea and China—were exposed to higher import costs and supply uncertainty. Europe faced pressure through fuel, freight and refined-product markets. Singapore and Rotterdam were exposed as major refining, trading and logistics hubs. These are representative transmission and exposure centres, not a claim that every listed city experienced identical physical damage or shortages.

title: The Mexican Peso Crisis (1994–1995)

epicentres.role: Policy and financial-market epicentre

entity: Government of Mexico; Banco de México; IMF; international investors
summary: In December 1994, Mexico devalued the peso after pressure on foreign-exchange reserves and the exchange-rate regime. Capital outflows, short-term dollar-linked public debt and declining confidence intensified the crisis. The peso fell sharply, financing conditions tightened and the shock spread to other emerging markets, becoming known as the Tequila Crisis.
why: The crisis showed how a fixed or tightly managed exchange-rate commitment can become vulnerable when reserves, fiscal credibility, short-term financing and investor confidence come under pressure. The structure of short-term dollar-linked debt made refinancing particularly difficult.
impact: Mexico faced recession, inflation and a severe squeeze on household purchasing power. Banks and businesses came under stress, while the United States and international institutions arranged emergency support. The episode also triggered wider reassessment of emerging-market risk.

title: The Asian Financial Crisis (1997–1998)

epicentres.role: Initial currency-crisis trigger
Major banking and currency crisis centre
Corporate and financial-sector crisis centre
Currency and capital-market stress centre

entity: Bank of Thailand; Bank Indonesia; Bank of Korea; Bank Negara Malaysia; IMF; regional governments
summary: The crisis began when Thailand abandoned its baht-dollar peg on 2 July 1997. Currency pressure and investor reassessment spread through Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia and other regional markets. Foreign-currency borrowing, short-term external debt, weak financial institutions and fragile exchange-rate arrangements amplified the shock. The crisis continued through 1998 and had spillovers beyond Asia.
why: The episode demonstrated how currency mismatches, leveraged borrowing and fragile banking systems can turn pressure on one currency into a regional financial crisis. National experiences and policy responses differed; the crisis was not a single identical event across every country.
impact: Businesses failed, banks were restructured, currencies depreciated and output contracted. Households experienced job losses and reduced incomes. The crisis also reshaped regional financial regulation, reserve management and debates about IMF crisis programmes.

title: The Russian Financial Crisis & LTCM Collapse (1998)

entity: Government of Russia; Central Bank of Russia; Long-Term Capital Management; Federal Reserve Bank of New York
summary: Russia devalued the rouble, restructured domestic government debt and declared a moratorium on some private external debt payments in August 1998. The turmoil caused investors to flee riskier assets. Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM), a highly leveraged hedge fund with large positions across global markets, suffered severe losses as normally related prices moved sharply apart. A private-sector recapitalisation was organised with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York facilitating discussions.
why: The episode illustrated how sovereign risk, market liquidity and highly leveraged financial institutions can interact. Positions that appear diversified under normal conditions may become correlated during a crisis, while forced selling can intensify market stress.
impact: Russian households and businesses faced inflation, financial disruption and loss of confidence. International markets experienced a flight to quality and wider credit spreads. The LTCM episode intensified scrutiny of leverage, counterparty exposures and systemic risk.

title: The Enron Corporate Accounting Scandal (2001)

epicentres.role: Enron headquarters and corporate reporting epicentre

entity: Enron Corporation; Arthur Andersen; U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission; investors and employees
summary: Enron disclosed a large quarterly loss in October 2001 and revealed accounting issues that undermined confidence in its reported earnings and financial position. The company had used complex structures and accounting practices to obscure debt and inflate performance. It filed for bankruptcy in December 2001, then the largest U.S. corporate bankruptcy at the time.
why: The scandal exposed weaknesses in corporate governance, auditor independence, disclosure and the oversight of off-balance-sheet entities. It showed how investors can be misled when financial statements do not present a clear picture of a company's obligations and risks.
impact: Employees lost jobs and retirement savings, shareholders suffered major losses, and confidence in corporate reporting was damaged. The scandal helped drive the Sarbanes–Oxley Act of 2002 and tighter requirements for audit committees, internal controls and financial disclosures.

title: The Argentine Debt Default & Peso Devaluation (2001–2002)

epicentres.role: Sovereign debt, banking and currency crisis centre

entity: Government of Argentina; Central Bank of Argentina; IMF; domestic and foreign creditors
summary: After years of recession and mounting debt pressures, Argentina defaulted on sovereign debt in December 2001. In early 2002 it abandoned the currency-board arrangement that had pegged the peso one-to-one with the U.S. dollar. The peso depreciated sharply, bank withdrawals were restricted and the financial system suffered a deep crisis.
why: The crisis reflected an increasingly unsustainable exchange-rate arrangement, rising public debt, weak growth and reduced access to external financing. The sudden end of convertibility exposed the risks of trying to maintain a currency peg without a supporting fiscal and economic framework.
impact: Output and incomes collapsed, poverty rose and savings were disrupted. Banks, businesses and households faced severe uncertainty as deposits and contracts were affected by emergency measures. The crisis became a major case study in sovereign debt restructuring and exchange-rate regimes.

summary: In June 2012, Barclays agreed to major regulatory settlements after investigations found that traders and submitters had attempted to manipulate submissions used to calculate the London Interbank Offered Rate (Libor). why: Libor relied on submissions from panel banks, creating opportunities for conflicts of interest and manipulation. The scandal exposed weaknesses in benchmark governance, internal controls and oversight of financial-market conduct.
impact: The case damaged public trust in banks and prompted criminal and regulatory investigations, fines and reforms to benchmark administration. Libor was subsequently phased out in major currencies and replaced by alternative reference rates.
